hints: Focus on electrons, since oxidation of the organic means reduction of dichromate, so start by counting how many electrons one mole of dichromate gains.
One mole of dichromate gains 6 electrons and oxidises three moles of X, so work out how many electrons each single molecule of X must lose.
For each option, count O atoms gained as 2 electrons each and H atoms lost as 1 electron each, and look for the change that loses exactly 2 electrons under reflux.
walkthrough:
**Find electrons gained by the oxidising agent**

Think of this as an electron trade. The dichromate is reduced, so it takes electrons from X.

Reduction half-equation:
$$\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{e}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
This tells us 1 mole of $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ gains 6 moles of electrons.

**Find electrons lost by each molecule of X**

We are told 1 mole of dichromate oxidises 3 moles of X. So the 6 electrons must come from 3 molecules of X.

Electrons per X:
$$\frac{6\text{ e}^-}{3 \text{ mol X}} = 2\text{ e}^- \text{ per molecule of X}$$
So X must undergo an oxidation that releases exactly 2 electrons.

**Translate [O] and [H] into electrons**

Use the two rules given in the question. Gaining one O atom releases 2 electrons, losing one H atom releases 1 electron.
$$\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow [\text{O}] + 2\text{H}^+ + 2\text{e}^-$$
$$[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{H}^+ + \text{e}^-$$
So we need a total change of $2\text{e}^-$: that is one [O] gained and no [H] lost.

**Test propanal under reflux**

Propanal is an aldehyde, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$. Under heating under reflux with excess hot acidified dichromate, it is oxidised once to propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$.

Change: gains 1 O atom, loses 0 net H for the functional group change $\text{CHO} \rightarrow \text{COOH}$.
$$\text{electrons lost} = 1 \times 2 = 2\text{e}^-$$
This matches perfectly, so propanal fits the 3:1 mole ratio.

options.A: Propanal $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ is oxidised to propanoic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ under reflux. This is gain of one [O] only, which releases 2 electrons. Since 3 moles of X release 3 x 2 = 6 electrons, this exactly matches the 6 electrons needed by 1 mole of dichromate.
options.B: Propan-1-ol $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ under reflux goes all the way to propanoic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. That is gain of 1 [O] (2e-) plus loss of 2 [H] (2e-), total 4 electrons per molecule. One mole of dichromate (6e-) would then oxidise only 1.5 moles, not 3 moles.
options.C: Propan-1,2-diol $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{OH}$ has two alcohol groups. The primary alcohol becomes a carboxylic acid (4e-) and the secondary alcohol becomes a ketone (loss of 2[H] = 2e-), giving $\text{CH}_3\text{COCOOH}$ in total. That is 6 electrons per molecule, so the ratio would be 1:1, not 3:1.
options.D: Propan-1,3-diol $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ has two primary alcohol groups. Under reflux both become carboxylic acids to give propanedioic acid $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{COOH}$. Each end loses 4 electrons, total 8 electrons per molecule. This is far more than the 2 electrons required.
